docs.text: Changelog All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file. @lambdaorm/lib 3.2.2 Patch Changes e4ce3af: 3xpr 5.2.0 in every package (one copy of it). lib builds each Orm's 3xpr instance with the ExpressionsBuilder 3xpr now exports, instead of importing it from one of its files. Updated dependencies [e4ce3af] @lambdaorm/base@3.2.1 3.2.1 Patch Changes 2dc1ac1: Fixes found running the same checks on every engine (engines lab, docs/PLAN.md B7): stage.fetch / push compare a column the way the dialect creates it: no false drift (and no needless ALTER ) for MySQL/MariaDB booleans, Oracle numbers and nullability, SQL Server and MariaDB json; MariaDB LONGTEXT is read. MySQL/MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle: in(p.x, list) with the list in a variable. json columns are read as objects also where the driver answers text (MariaDB, Oracle CLOB ); SQL Server writes them. SQL Server: delete with a filter ( DELETE c FROM t c ). Oracle: autoIncrement columns are identity columns; booleans are written as Y / N . MongoDB: transactions commit and roll back (the session was not used), update/delete answer the matched/deleted documents, autoIncrement keys, string literals and '' in filters, json values, in with a list, include of a composite relation, and update().include() of a composite saves the embedded children. upsert on SQL Server, Oracle and MongoDB says it is not supported yet. 68faedb: Each Orm has its own 3xpr instance. With the shared one, every new Orm() replaced orm.execute (and the other orm.* functions): the listeners and scripts of an earlier Orm ran their queries on the last one created, outside their own transaction. 3.2.0 Minor Changes 7c18bef: - A filter by a field of a relation whose entity lives in another source works (L15): QuoteLines.filter(p => p.deviceModel.name == name) first queries DeviceModels on its source and then filters QuoteLines with in(p.deviceModelId, …) . Each comparison is solved on its own ( && , || , ! keep their meaning); the other side must be a value (a clear error otherwise) and only one level of relation is supported. PostgreSQL: in(p.x, list) / p.x.in(list) with the list in a variable works — the parameter was typed as its elements and the array was sent as a Postgres array literal (L33). 38e7d3b: New orm.executeScript(script, data, options) : evaluates a 3xpr script whose orm.execute(query, data, options) calls all run in one transaction, also across sources. The script can use variables, if , for , for … in , throw , try / catch and return ; it commits when it ends and rolls back and rejects when anything fails (a query, a function or a throw ). It works on a copy of data , cannot read environment variables, and its orm.execute calls without a stage run on the script's stage. Returns the value of the last statement (or of return ). js const quoteId = await orm.executeScript( ` orm.execute("Quotes.insert()", { id: quoteId, accountId: accountId, status: "draft" }); for (line in lines) { orm.execute("QuoteLines.insert()", { id: line.id, quoteId: quoteId, deviceModelId: line.modelId, quantity: line.qty }); } orm.execute("Accounts.update(p => ({ lastQuoteAt: now() })).filter(p => p.id == accountId)", { accountId: accountId }); quoteId `, { quoteId, accountId, lines } ); 3f3e1cc: Listeners ( application.listeners ) are awaited one after the other and run in the sentence's transaction: their orm.execute calls use the same connections, an error in before prevents the sentence, an error in after fails it, and a rollback undoes what they wrote. A sentence with listeners that runs on its own opens a transaction for itself and its listeners. They used to run detached ( forEach(async …) ): execute could return before them, their errors escaped as uncaught exceptions and they wrote outside the transaction — L10. New listener option transactional: false (base ListenerConfig ): the listener runs outside the transaction, and what it writes is kept even if the sentence's transaction rolls back. c2be59f: push compares the model with the databases (as fetch reads them), not with orm_state — L19: a new environment or a CI runner without the last push's orm_state no longer gets CREATE TABLE for tables that exist. Tables missing in the database are created with their keys, FKs and indexes; in existing tables, missing columns are added ( ADD COLUMN , L27), columns with another type, length or nullability are altered, and a property mapping with previousMapping: <old column> renames the column ( ALTER TABLE … RENAME COLUMN , L20; SqlServer sp_rename ). Nothing that exists only in the database is dropped ( stage.fetch() reports it). orm_state is still written by push as a record. d16b60a: stage.push().sentencesBySource() : the DDL grouped per source (one script per database). cli: lambdaorm push -o <dir> writes one script per source that changes, <stage>.<source>.sql (deterministic names, to rename into a versioned migration); -o without a folder prints the DDL grouped by source — L19. e961817: update().include(p => p.children) on a composite relation saves the aggregate: the children sent are inserted or updated (upsert by primary key, with the parent's key), and the parent's children that were not sent are deleted. Children absent from the data are not touched. It used to update only the existing children that were sent — L17. Supported where upsert is (PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB); SqlServer, Oracle and SQLjs report it as not supported yet (MongoDB keeps composite children embedded). An explicit include(p => p.children.update(…)) keeps updating only. 8b8f470: Stage commands: push/DDL: a stage's last source without condition is a catch-all, as in DML: it gets only the entities no other source took (it used to receive every entity) — L25. fetch/pull on PostgreSQL work with reserved words as column names ( order ): the metadata query quoted the column twice — L6, L21. stage.fetch() reports the drift: per mapping, the entities that differ from the model (present in one side only, different columns, types, lengths, required, primary key), each with its differences ; no entities when in step. stage.read() returns the databases' mappings as fetch did (pull uses it) — L22. cli: lambdaorm fetch exits with code 1 when there are differences (for CI). fetch , pull , schema , introspect and incorporate load the --envfile they declared (it was ignored). 907074b: Transactions: orm.transaction now waits for the transaction: it resolves after the commit and rejects with the callback's error after the rollback (the error used to escape as an uncaught exception and the promise resolved undefined ) — L26. If the rollback itself fails, the callback's error is still the one reported. Everything executed inside orm.transaction joins it, also when it doesn't go through tr : orm.execute , repositories, the orm.execute function of an expression. It runs on the transaction's connections (one per source), so a rollback undoes it — L31. A nested orm.transaction joins the outer one, a query with include no longer opens a second transaction, and an execution on another stage inside a transaction fails with a clear error. Each Orm instance keeps its own transaction context. 7c8edd7: Types and values: New property type json (L1): objects and lists are written as JSON and come back as objects and lists. Column type: PostgreSQL JSONB , MySQL/MariaDB JSON , SqlServer NVARCHAR(MAX) , Oracle CLOB , others TEXT . A list is no longer sent as a Postgres array literal. The mapping's dbType reaches the DDL when a table or column is created or altered (it was used in one place only) — e.g. dbType: timestamptz(3) (L1, L2). PostgreSQL writes dateTime with milliseconds and the offset ( yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSSZZ ): milliseconds are kept and a timestamptz column stores the exact instant; timestamp columns keep storing the local time (L2). '' , 0 and false parameters are values: only undefined becomes NULL (an empty string used to be written as NULL, and so were 0 and false ) — L3. (The "" literal needs 3xpr 5.1.1.) A string property without length is no longer given length 80 in the model: PostgreSQL creates TEXT , the other dialects keep VARCHAR(80) — L24. On PostgreSQL, the next push of an existing model widens those columns to TEXT. de140f3: update answers the number of affected rows (as delete does, and as the repositories' update(): Promise<number> always declared); it answered { data: <parameters> } . Lets callers detect "not found" (0) and optimistic-lock conflicts ( filter(p => p.id == id && p.version == version) → 0) — L4. SQLjs update / delete now return the modified rows too. 6319468: Entity.upsert() : insert, or update the row with the same primary key, in one sentence — PostgreSQL INSERT … ON CONFLICT (pk) DO UPDATE SET c = EXCLUDED.c , MySQL/MariaDB ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE c = VALUES(c) (other dialects: a clear "not supported" error). Written like an insert ( upsert() , upsert(entity) , upsert({ … }) ); answers the data like insert — L18. It used to fail with function: upsert not found . Patch Changes 2ee8930: Upgrade the data7expressions dependencies to their latest major: 3xpr from 1.x to ^5.1.1 , h3lp and typ3s to ^5.0.0 (and json-light to ^5.0.0 in the CLI). No API changes were needed. Behaviour inherited from 3xpr: <= now has the same precedence as the other comparison operators ( a <= b == true used to evaluate as a <= (b == true) ). 3xpr 5.1.0 evaluates async expressions statement by statement (listeners, orm.execute inside expressions), never runs an async function while building an expression, and adds throw , try / catch , return , break and continue ; 3xpr 5.1.1 parses the empty string literal "" (it used to swallow the rest of the expression). ee1e7ac: Packaging: The published exports pointed to ./build/lib/index.js , a path the package doesn't have: require('@lambdaorm/lib') (and base, client) failed for everyone installing from npm. dist now rewrites exports (and bin ) like main — L7. cli: declares bin: lambdaorm , so npm i -g @lambdaorm/cli installs the lambdaorm command — L29. Every package's dist is smoke-tested before it can be released: required by its name (so exports applies) and, for the CLI, lambdaorm --help . b1dcd8b: - orm.executeScript(script, data, options, { timeout }) : when the timeout passes the script's transaction rolls back and the promise rejects. A finished transaction (committed or rolled back) refuses any later execution, so work that outlives it (a script that timed out, a kept tr ) never reaches the database. ExecutionError keeps the database's error code ( error.code , e.g. Postgres 23505 ); it used to be lost. Repositories Repositories are associated with an entity and have several methods to interact with the entity. Example: import { orm } from 'lambdaorm' import { ProductRepository } from './models/northwind' (async () => { await orm.init() const productRepository = new ProductRepository('mydb') const country = 'USA' const result = await productRepository.query().filter(p => (p.price > 5 && p.supplier.country === country) || (p.inStock < 3)) .having(p => max(p.price) > 50) .map(p => ({ category: p.category.name, largestPrice: max(p.price) })) .sort(p => desc(p.largestPrice)) .execute({ country: country }) console.log(JSON.stringify(result, null, 2)) await orm.end() })() method Description insert To insert one record bulkInsert To insert records update To update one record updateAll to be able to update all the records of an entity delete To delete one record deleteAll delete all records of an entity get get one record first returns the first record last returns the last record take returns one record query permite realizar una consulta personalizada The repositories are generated by lambdaorm by executing the update command. When executing this command, among other tasks, a repository is created for each entity of the defined schemas. These files are only generated the first time, so it is safe to add custom methods to these repositories. Example: import { Repository, IOrm } from 'lambdaorm' import { Product, QryProduct } from './model' export class ProductRepository extends Repository<Product, QryProduct> { constructor (database?: string, Orm?:IOrm) { super('Products', database, Orm) } // Add your methods here }

docs.text: Script A script is a small program, written in 3xpr (a JavaScript-like expression language), that λORM runs with orm.executeScript(script, data, options) . Inside it, orm.execute(query, data, options) runs λORM queries, and variables, conditions and loops decide which ones and with what data. What it is for Many use cases are more than one query: place an order (the order, its lines, the customer's balance), move stock between warehouses, register a payment and its audit. Their writes must happen completely or not at all : an order without its lines, or a balance discounted for an order that was not saved, is a corrupt state. orm.transaction(callback) solves it in Node code. A script solves it in a single call that carries the whole use case , wherever the call comes from: Node ( orm.executeScript ), the Data Gateway ( POST /script ), the client ( @lambdaorm/client ) or the CLI ( lambdaorm script ). A client in any language can run a use case with several reads and writes in one transaction, which it could not do sending one query per request. Features All or nothing : everything the script executes is one transaction — committed when it ends, rolled back if anything fails (a query, a throw , the timeout). See below . Across sources and stages : queries on several databases, and on another stage with orm.execute(query, data, { stage: "insights" }) , are part of the same transaction. Listeners included : what the schema's listeners write is committed or undone with the script. A language, not only queries : variables, if , for , while , switch , try/catch , throw , return , list functions ( filter , map , sum , …) and every function of 3xpr and λORM. Read your writes : a statement sees what the previous ones wrote, before the commit. A result : the value of the last statement (or of return ) — a value, a row, an object built by the script. Safe for scripts sent by clients : no access to environment variables, works on a copy of data , timeout and maxIterations stop it (also a loop that never ends), and the Data Gateway runs scripts only when its configuration enables them ( scripts.enabled ) and the credential has the script permission. A first look — the examples go step by step, from a single query to a complete use case: const total = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); for (l in lines) { orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty }); } lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price) `, { orderId, lines }, { stage: 'default' } ) The main feature: all or nothing Everything a script executes is one transaction. Every orm.execute of the script — on one source or on several, on the script's stage or on another one, and what the listeners write — runs on the same connections: when the script ends, everything is committed ; if anything fails — a query, a function, a rule that throw s, the timeout — everything the script did is rolled back , in every source and stage, and the promise rejects with that error. That is what a script is for: a use case with several reads and writes (an order with its lines, a stock movement, a transfer) that must happen completely or not at all , in a single call — also from the Data Gateway ( POST /script ), the client or the CLI , where a client could otherwise only send one query per request and could not undo the previous ones. When the script… Result ends normally commit of everything; resolves with the last value (or return ) throws ( throw ) rollback of everything; rejects with that error runs a query that fails (e.g. a duplicate key) rollback of everything; rejects with the database's error catches an error with try/catch it goes on; the error does not undo anything by itself passes timeout or maxIterations it stops, rollback of everything; rejects Arguments Argument Description script The 3xpr script data The variables of the script. The script works on a copy: data is never changed options The query options plus the script's limits ( ScriptOptions ), see below Option Description stage The stage of the transaction and of every orm.execute without a stage timeout Max time in ms: when it passes, the loops stop, the transaction rolls back and the script rejects maxIterations Max loop iterations of the script, all loops together; past it the script fails and rolls back Up to @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0 the limits were a fourth argument ( executeScript(script, data, options, { timeout, maxIterations }) ); since 3.4.0 everything goes in options . Examples Each example says what it does and what happens when it fails. The model of the examples domain: entities: - name: Customers primaryKey: [id] uniqueKey: [code] properties: - { name: id, type: integer, required: true, autoIncrement: true } - { name: code, length: 20, required: true } - { name: name, required: true } - { name: notes } - { name: balance, type: decimal } - name: Orders primaryKey: [id] properties: - { name: id, length: 36, required: true } - { name: customerId, type: integer } - { name: status, length: 20, required: true } - { name: version, type: integer, required: true } relations: - { name: lines, type: manyToOne, composite: true, from: id, entity: OrderLines, to: orderId } - name: OrderLines primaryKey: [orderId, line] properties: - { name: orderId, length: 36, required: true } - { name: line, type: integer, required: true } - { name: product, length: 40, required: true } - { name: quantity, type: integer } - name: AuditLogs primaryKey: [id] properties: - { name: id, type: integer, required: true, autoIncrement: true } - { name: entityName, length: 40 } - { name: refId, length: 36 } The examples run on the stage default ; examples 11 and 13 also write on a stage insights . They are the engines lab model, where the same scripts are tested on PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle and MongoDB. 1. A single query The simplest script is one orm.execute . The script returns the value of its last statement — here the rows of the query. Even this runs in a transaction (it opens, the query runs, it commits). const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: code }) `, { code }, { stage: 'default' } ) 2. Several statements, in order Statements run one after the other, each orm.execute awaited before the next. A statement sees what the previous ones wrote, before the commit (they share the connection). const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: name }); orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code).map(p => p.name)", { code: code }) `, { code, name: 'Ana' }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: [{ name: "Ana" }]. 3. Using the result of a statement Assign a result to a variable and use it below. An insert answers { data } with the values written, generated ones included: customer.data.id is the id the database generated. const result = await orm.executeScript(` customer = orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: name }); orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, customerId: customer.data.id, status: "new", version: 1 }); customer.data.id `, { code, name: 'Ana', orderId }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: the id generated for the customer. 4. Affected rows: "not found" as an error update and delete answer the number of affected rows. A script can turn 0 into an error; throw with a status is answered with that HTTP status by the Data Gateway. const result = await orm.executeScript(` updated = orm.execute("Customers.update(p => ({ name: name })).filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: code, name: name }); if (updated == 0) { throw { status: 404, message: "customer " + code + " not found" }; } updated `, { code: 'missing', name: 'Bob' }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: rejects: customer missing not found (404). 5. Conditions: create only what is missing if with a query in the condition. Run it twice with the same data: the second time it creates nothing. const result = await orm.executeScript(` created = 0; for (c in customers) { if (orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: c.code }).length() == 0) { orm.execute("Customers.insert()", c); created += 1; } } created `, { customers: [{ code: 'c1', name: 'Ana' }, { code: 'c2', name: 'Bob' }] }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: 2 the first time, 0 the second. 6. Loops: one row per item for (item in list) over the data. Every insert of the loop is in the same transaction: all the lines are written, or none. Lists also have filter , map , sum , count … const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); for (l in lines) { orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty }); } lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price) `, { orderId, lines: [{ line: 1, product: 'camera', qty: 2, price: 10 }, { line: 2, product: 'hub', qty: 1, price: 5 }] }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: 25. 7. Aggregates with include A composite relation can be written with include , as in orm.execute outside a script. Here the order and its lines in one sentence, then read back with its lines. const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert().include(p => p.lines)", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1, lines: lines.map(l => ({ orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty })) }); orders = orm.execute("Orders.filter(p => p.id == orderId).include(p => p.lines)", { orderId: orderId }); orders[0].lines.length() `, { orderId, lines: [{ line: 1, product: 'camera', qty: 2 }, { line: 2, product: 'hub', qty: 1 }] }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: 2. 8. A business rule: throw, and everything is undone The rule is checked after writing: the order and its lines are already in the database (inside the transaction). throw stops the script and rolls back everything it wrote : no order and no line is left. const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); for (l in lines) { orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty }); } total = lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price); if (total > maxTotal) { throw { status: 400, message: "the order exceeds " + maxTotal }; } total `, { orderId, maxTotal: 20, lines: [ …total 25… ] }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: rejects: the order exceeds 20 (400); the order and its lines are not in the database. 9. Handling an error: try / catch An error caught with try/catch does not abort the script: it goes on and commits. Use it for optional steps; any error not caught rolls everything back. const result = await orm.executeScript(` try { if (vip) { throw "vip customers are reviewed by hand"; } note = "ok"; } catch (e) { note = e.message; } orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: name, notes: note }); note `, { code, name: 'Ana', vip: true }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: "vip customers are reviewed by hand" (and the customer is written). 10. Listeners run inside the script's transaction A schema listener (here, one that writes an AuditLogs row after each order insert) runs in the script's transaction: committed with it, and undone with it if the script fails. application: listeners: - name: auditOrders on: [insert] condition: entity == "Orders" after: orm.execute("AuditLogs.insert()", { entityName: "Orders", refId: data.id }) const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); throw "cancel"; `, { orderId }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: rejects: cancel; neither the order nor its audit row are in the database. 11. Another stage in the same transaction orm.execute(query, data, { stage: "insights" }) runs on another stage — other sources, even another database engine — in the same transaction : if anything fails afterwards, the write on the other stage is undone too. const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); orm.execute("AuditLogs.insert()", { entityName: "new order", refId: orderId }, { stage: insights }); if (fail) { throw "something failed after both writes"; } "done" `, { orderId, insights: 'insights', fail: true }, { stage: 'default' } ) Result: rejects; the order (default stage) and the audit row (insights stage) are both undone. 12. Limits: timeout and maxIterations Options of the script, with the stage: timeout (ms) stops it — also a loop that never ends — and rolls back; maxIterations caps the loop iterations of the whole script. Both are worth setting when scripts come from clients. const result = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Customers.insert()", { code: code, name: "never kept" }); while (true) { x = 1; } `, { code }, { stage: 'default', timeout: 2000, maxIterations: 10000 } ) Result: rejects (maxIterations, or the timeout first); the customer is not written. 13. A complete use case: place an order Everything together: validate, write an aggregate, apply a rule, write on another stage and answer a summary. One call, one transaction — if any step fails, nothing of the order exists anywhere . const result = await orm.executeScript(` customers = orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == customerCode)", { customerCode: customerCode }); if (customers.length() == 0) { throw { status: 404, message: "customer " + customerCode + " not found" }; } customer = customers[0]; orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, customerId: customer.id, status: "new", version: 1 }); for (l in lines) { orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty }); } total = lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price); if (total > customer.balance) { throw { status: 409, message: "insufficient balance" }; } orm.execute("Customers.update(p => ({ balance: balance })).filter(p => p.id == id)", { id: customer.id, balance: customer.balance - total }); orm.execute("AuditLogs.insert()", { entityName: "order total " + total, refId: orderId }, { stage: insights }); { orderId: orderId, total: total, balance: customer.balance - total } `, { customerCode: 'c1', orderId, insights: 'insights', lines: [{ line: 1, product: 'camera', qty: 2, price: 10 }, { line: 2, product: 'hub', qty: 1, price: 5 }] }, { stage: 'default', timeout: 10000, maxIterations: 10000 } ) Result: { orderId, total: 25, balance: 75 } with a balance of 100; with a balance of 20 it rejects (409) and the order, its lines, the balance and the audit row are left as they were. 14. Another use case: a quote with its total on insights A quote with its lines on the main stage and its total on the insights stage (other sources, possibly another database), in one transaction. The account must exist; if any step fails, neither the quote, nor its lines, nor the total are left anywhere. (A model with Accounts , Quotes , QuoteLines and QuoteTotals .) const quoteId = await orm.executeScript(` account = orm.execute("Accounts.filter(p => p.id == accountId)", { accountId: accountId }); if (account.length() == 0) { throw { status: 404, message: "account not found" }; } orm.execute("Quotes.insert()", { id: quoteId, accountId: accountId, status: "draft" }); for (line in lines) { orm.execute("QuoteLines.insert()", { id: line.id, quoteId: quoteId, productId: line.productId, quantity: line.qty }); } total = lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price); orm.execute("QuoteTotals.insert()", { quoteId: quoteId, total: total }, { stage: "insights" }); quoteId `, { quoteId, accountId, lines }, { stage: 'default', timeout: 10000, maxIterations: 10000 } ) The same script from a client The script and its data are the same everywhere; only the call changes. // @lambdaorm/client, against a Data Gateway import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/client' await orm.init('http://localhost:8080', { headers: { 'X-Api-Key': process.env.BACKEND_KEY } }) const result = await orm.executeScript(script, data, { stage: 'default', timeout: 10000 }) # REST: a Data Gateway with scripts.enabled and a credential with the script permission curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/script -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "X-Api-Key: $BACKEND_KEY" \ -d '{ "script": "orm.execute(\"Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)\", { code: code })", "data": { "code": "c1" }, "options": { "stage": "default" } }' # CLI: a script file, data as JSON lambdaorm script -f place-order.3xpr -d '{ "customerCode": "c1", "orderId": "o-1", "lines": [] }' -s default The language Everything 3xpr has: Variables: total = 0; , objects { id: id, name: "x" } , lists [1, 2] , items[0].name . if / else if / else , while , for (i = 0; i < n; i += 1) , for (item in items) , switch / case , break , continue , return . throw "message" ; try { … } catch (e) { e.message } . throw { status: 404, message: "…" } makes the Data Gateway answer with that status; in Node the error's message is that object as JSON. Arrow functions as arguments: items.filter(p => p.qty > 1).map(p => p.name) , items.sum(p => p.qty) , items.each(p => …) . 3xpr's functions: strings ( upper , concat , …), numbers, dates ( now() , …), lists, nvl , iif , … (see Operators & Functions ). Not available: the ? : operator ( iif(c, a, b) evaluates both sides), ++ / -- (use i += 1 ) and declaring functions. Statements run in order, and each orm.execute is awaited before the next statement. Plus the functions λORM adds: Function Description orm.execute(query, data, options) Executes a query in the script's transaction; options.stage may name another stage (same transaction) orm.plan(query, options) The plan of a query ( .sentence , …) orm.parameters(query) The parameters of a query orm.metadata(query) The metadata of a query orm.model(query) The model (fields) a query returns orm.constraints(query) The constraints a query checks toBase64(value) / getBase64(value) "abc" → "YWJj" and back encrypt(value, key) / decrypt(value, key) AES Writing scripts: a few rules Statements end with ; ; the last one (without ; ) is the result. return value; ends the script early. Variables need no declaration: total = 0; . data is copied: the script never changes the caller's object. Count with i += 1 (there is no ++ ); use iif(condition, a, b) (there is no ? : ). A query's result can be indexed directly: orm.execute("Customers.filter(p => p.code == code)", { code: code })[0].name ; an empty list is [] (both need 3xpr 5.3.1, from @lambdaorm/lib 3.4.1). A script can't read environment variables ( $VAR ). Transaction and stages One transaction for the whole script, also across sources and stages: commit at the end; rollback and reject on any error. orm.execute(query, data) without stage runs on the stage of options ; with { stage: "insights" } it runs on that stage, in the same transaction (since @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0). A statement sees what the previous ones wrote (same connection), before the commit. There is no two-phase commit: with several databases the commit goes source by source. Security and limits The script cannot read environment variables ( $VAR fails), so it can't read connection strings. timeout : when it passes, the script's loops stop, the transaction rolls back and the script rejects; whatever it still executes afterwards fails without reaching the database. maxIterations : the loop iterations of the script, all loops together; past it the script fails and rolls back. The Data Gateway uses scripts.maxIterations (default 100000). Since @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0 (3xpr 5.3.0) a while (true) {} no longer blocks the process: the timeout and maxIterations stop it. In the Data Gateway scripts are off by default ( scripts.enabled ) and need the script permission.
docs.title: Script

docs.text: A script is a small program, written in 3xpr (a JavaScript-like expression language), that λORM runs with orm.executeScript(script, data, options) . Inside it, orm.execute(query, data, options) runs λORM queries, and variables, conditions and loops decide which ones and with what data.
docs.title: Script

docs.text: Many use cases are more than one query: place an order (the order, its lines, the customer's balance), move stock between warehouses, register a payment and its audit. Their writes must happen completely or not at all : an order without its lines, or a balance discounted for an order that was not saved, is a corrupt state. orm.transaction(callback) solves it in Node code. A script solves it in a single call that carries the whole use case , wherever the call comes from: Node ( orm.executeScript ), the Data Gateway ( POST /script ), the client ( @lambdaorm/client ) or the CLI ( lambdaorm script ). A client in any language can run a use case with several reads and writes in one transaction, which it could not do sending one query per request.
docs.title: What it is for

docs.text: All or nothing : everything the script executes is one transaction — committed when it ends, rolled back if anything fails (a query, a throw , the timeout). See below . Across sources and stages : queries on several databases, and on another stage with orm.execute(query, data, { stage: "insights" }) , are part of the same transaction. Listeners included : what the schema's listeners write is committed or undone with the script. A language, not only queries : variables, if , for , while , switch , try/catch , throw , return , list functions ( filter , map , sum , …) and every function of 3xpr and λORM. Read your writes : a statement sees what the previous ones wrote, before the commit. A result : the value of the last statement (or of return ) — a value, a row, an object built by the script. Safe for scripts sent by clients : no access to environment variables, works on a copy of data , timeout and maxIterations stop it (also a loop that never ends), and the Data Gateway runs scripts only when its configuration enables them ( scripts.enabled ) and the credential has the script permission. A first look — the examples go step by step, from a single query to a complete use case: const total = await orm.executeScript(` orm.execute("Orders.insert()", { id: orderId, status: "new", version: 1 }); for (l in lines) { orm.execute("OrderLines.insert()", { orderId: orderId, line: l.line, product: l.product, quantity: l.qty }); } lines.sum(p => p.qty * p.price) `, { orderId, lines }, { stage: 'default' } )
docs.title: Features

docs.text: Everything a script executes is one transaction. Every orm.execute of the script — on one source or on several, on the script's stage or on another one, and what the listeners write — runs on the same connections: when the script ends, everything is committed ; if anything fails — a query, a function, a rule that throw s, the timeout — everything the script did is rolled back , in every source and stage, and the promise rejects with that error. That is what a script is for: a use case with several reads and writes (an order with its lines, a stock movement, a transfer) that must happen completely or not at all , in a single call — also from the Data Gateway ( POST /script ), the client or the CLI , where a client could otherwise only send one query per request and could not undo the previous ones. When the script… Result ends normally commit of everything; resolves with the last value (or return ) throws ( throw ) rollback of everything; rejects with that error runs a query that fails (e.g. a duplicate key) rollback of everything; rejects with the database's error catches an error with try/catch it goes on; the error does not undo anything by itself passes timeout or maxIterations it stops, rollback of everything; rejects
docs.title: The main feature: all or nothing

docs.text: Argument Description script The 3xpr script data The variables of the script. The script works on a copy: data is never changed options The query options plus the script's limits ( ScriptOptions ), see below Option Description stage The stage of the transaction and of every orm.execute without a stage timeout Max time in ms: when it passes, the loops stop, the transaction rolls back and the script rejects maxIterations Max loop iterations of the script, all loops together; past it the script fails and rolls back Up to @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0 the limits were a fourth argument ( executeScript(script, data, options, { timeout, maxIterations }) ); since 3.4.0 everything goes in options .

docs.text: Transaction To work with transactions use the orm.transaction(options, callback) method. It receives the options (the stage, { stage: 'default' } ) and a callback that receives a transaction object, in the examples named tr . When the callback ends the orm commits; if it throws, the orm rolls back. Behaviour The promise resolves after the commit and rejects with the callback's error after the rollback . If the rollback itself fails, the callback's error is still the one reported. Everything executed inside the callback joins the transaction : tr.execute , orm.execute , repositories, the orm.execute of a listener or of an expression. It runs on the transaction's connections (one per source), so a rollback undoes it in every source. A nested orm.transaction joins the outer one: one commit, done by the outer. An execution without stage runs on the transaction's stage. An execution with another stage joins the transaction too (since @lambdaorm/lib 3.3.0): every stage shares the transaction's connections and they commit or roll back together. A finished transaction refuses later executions. There is no two-phase commit: with several databases the commit goes source by source; if a later commit fails the earlier ones stay. To send several queries in one transaction from a single call (also over REST), see Script . await orm.transaction({ stage: 'default' }, async tr => { await tr.execute('Quotes.insert()', quote) // orm.execute inside the callback also joins the transaction await orm.execute('Accounts.update(p => ({ lastQuoteAt: at })).filter(p => p.id == id)', { id: quote.accountId, at: new Date() }) // another stage: same transaction await tr.execute('QuoteSummaries.insert()', summary, { stage: 'insights' }) }) Example: import { orm } from '../../lib' import { Orders } from '../northwind/model/__model' (async () => { try { await orm.init('./config/northwind.yaml') const order = { customerId: 'VINET', employeeId: 5, orderDate: '1996-07-03T22:00:00.000Z', requiredDate: '1996-07-31T22:00:00.000Z', shippedDate: '1996-07-15T22:00:00.000Z', shipViaId: 3, freight: 32.38, name: 'Vins et alcools Chevalier', address: '59 rue de l-Abbaye', city: 'Reims', region: null, postalCode: '51100', country: 'France', details: [{ productId: 11, unitPrice: 14, quantity: 12, discount: !1 }, { productId: 42, unitPrice: 9.8, quantity: 10, discount: !1 }, { productId: 72, unitPrice: 34.8, quantity: 5, discount: !1 }] } await orm.transaction({ stage: 'source' }, async (tr) => { // create order const orderId = await tr.execute(() => Orders.insert().include(p => p.details), order) // get order const result = await tr.execute((id: number) => Orders.filter(p => p.id === id).include(p => p.details), { id: orderId }) const order2 = result[0] // updated order order2.address = 'changed 59 rue de l-Abbaye' order2.details[0].discount = true order2.details[1].unitPrice = 10 order2.details[2].quantity = 7 const updateCount = await tr.execute(() => Orders.update().include(p => p.details), order2) console.log(updateCount) // get order const order3 = await tr.execute((id: number) => Orders.filter(p => p.id === id).include(p => p.details), { id: orderId }) console.log(JSON.stringify(order3)) // delete const deleteCount = await tr.execute(() => Orders.delete().include(p => p.details), order3[0]) console.log(deleteCount) // get order const order4 = await tr.execute((id: number) => Orders.filter(p => p.id === id).include(p => p.details), { id: orderId }) console.log(JSON.stringify(order4)) }) } catch (error:any) { console.error(error.stack) } finally { // Ending the ORM connection await orm.end() } })()

docs.title: Behaviour

docs.text: To show different ways of consuming the ORM we will propose different cases with an example domain and we will propose different infrastructures. To simplify the schema, we will omit the specification of the properties, keys, indices and relationships of the entities as well as the mapping. But you can see the complete schema in the example labs. Unique Source Schema: In the following schema we define 4 entities in the domain: Categories, Customers, Products and Orders, with Orders being an entity composed of Orders and Order Details. In infrastructure we define a single scenario that is associated with a single data source called Ordering, which is a MySQL database, which uses the default mapping. domain: entities: - name: Categories - name: Customers - name: Products - name: Orders - name: Orders.details infrastructure: mappings: - name: default sources: - name: Ordering mapping: default dialect: MySQL connection: ${CNN_MYSQL} stages: - name: default sources: - name: Ordering Query: We will write the query to obtain an Order with its details belonging to a client. We will write the query using lambda expression. import { orm } from 'lambdaorm' import { Orders } from './northwind/domain/model' ( async () => { try { // Initialize the ORM by passing the schema file await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') // Query const query = (customerId:string)=> Orders.filter(p =>p.customerId==customerId) .include(p=>[p.customer.map(p=>p.name),p.details .include(p=>p.product .include(p=>p.category.map(p=>p.name)) .map(p=>p.name)) .map(p=>[p.quantity,p.unitPrice])]) .page(1,1) // Execute the query const result = await orm.execute(query, {customerId: 'CENTC' }) // Print the result console.log(JSON.stringify(result,null,2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error) } })() Result: [ { "id": 12, "customerId": "CENTC", "orderDate": "1996-07-18T00:00:00.000Z", "customer": { "name": "Centro comercial Moctezuma" }, "details": [ { "quantity": 10, "unitPrice": 8, "product": { "name": "Sir Rodney's Scones", "category": { "name": "Confections" } } }, { "quantity": 1, "unitPrice": 20.8, "product": { "name": "Gravad lax", "category": { "name": "Seafood" } } } ] } ] Multiple Sources Schema: In this case we will define a scenario where the domain entities are persisted in different data sources: The Categories, Products entities are persisted in the source Catalog, which is a MySQL database that uses the default mapping. The Customers entity is persisted in the Crm source, which is a PostgreSQL database that uses the default mapping. The Orders entity is persisted in the Ordering source, which is a MongoDB database that uses the mongoDb mapping. domain: entities: - name: Categories - name: Customers - name: Products - name: Orders - name: Orders.details infrastructure: mappings: - name: default - name: mongoDb extends: default sources: - name: Catalog dialect: MySQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_MYSQL} - name: Crm dialect: PostgreSQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_POSTGRES} - name: Ordering dialect: MongoDB mapping: mongoDb connection: ${CNN_MONGODB} stages: - name: default sources: - name: Catalog condition: entity.in(["Categories","Products"]) - name: Crm condition: entity.in(["Address","Customers"]) - name: Ordering condition: entity.in(["Orders","Orders.details"]) Query: This time we will execute the query from the command line interface (CLI) and we will obtain the same result as in the previous case. lambdaorm execute -e ".env" -q "Orders.filter(p => p.customerId == customerId).include(p => [p.customer.map(p => p.name), p.details.include(p => p.product.include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name)).map(p => p.name)).map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice])]).page(1,1)" -d "{\"customerId\": \"HANAR\"}" Result: [ { "id": 12, "customerId": "CENTC", "orderDate": "1996-07-18T00:00:00.000Z", "customer": { "name": "Centro comercial Moctezuma" }, "details": [ { "quantity": 10, "unitPrice": 8, "product": { "name": "Sir Rodney's Scones", "category": { "name": "Confections" } } }, { "quantity": 1, "unitPrice": 20.8, "product": { "name": "Gravad lax", "category": { "name": "Seafood" } } } ] } ] view complete laboratory CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) Schema: In this case we will define 3 scenarios for the same domain. default: where data is read and written to the Catalog, Crm and Ordering sources. insights: where the data from the Insights source is read and written. cqrs: where data is read from the Insights source but persisted in the Catalog, Crm and Ordering sources. In order to synchronize the data between the Catalog, Crm and Ordering sources with Insights, we will define a listener that will be executed after each insertion, update or deletion of data in the default and cqrs scenario and will apply the same operation in the insights scenario. domain: entities: - name: Categories - name: Customers - name: Products - name: Orders - name: Orders.details infrastructure: mappings: - name: default - name: mongoDb extends: default sources: - name: Catalog dialect: MySQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_MYSQL} - name: Crm dialect: PostgreSQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_POSTGRES} - name: Ordering dialect: MongoDB mapping: mongoDb connection: ${CNN_MONGODB} - name: Insights dialect: PostgreSQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_INSIGHTS} stages: - name: default sources: - name: Catalog condition: entity.in(["Categories","Products"]) - name: Crm condition: entity.in(["Address","Customers"]) - name: Ordering condition: entity.in(["Orders","Orders.details"]) - name: insights sources: - name: Insights - name: cqrs sources: - name: Insights condition: action == "select" - name: Catalog condition: entity.in(["Categories","Products"]) - name: Crm condition: entity.in(["Address","Customers"]) - name: Ordering condition: entity.in(["Orders","Orders.details"]) application: listeners: - name: syncInsights on: [insert, bulkInsert, update, delete ] condition: options.stage.in("default","cqrs") after: orm.execute(query,data,{stage:"insights"}) Query: In this case we will execute the query on a Data Gateway . curl -X POST "http://localhost:8080/execute?format=beautiful" -H "X-Api-Key: $KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"query": And configure Kafka consumers to update the data in the insights scenario. Schema: ... infrastructure: ... queue: config: $QUEUE_CONFIG consumers: - name: syncInsights config: groupId: group1 subscribe: topic: insights-sync fromBeginning: true execute: orm.execute(message.query,message.data, {stage:"insights"}) application: listeners: - name: syncInsights on: [insert, bulkInsert, update, delete ] condition: options.stage.in("default","cqrs") after: queue.send("insights-sync",[{query,data}]) Node Client Schema: In the case of using a client, the schema only defines the domain and the paths in the infrastructure, since the sources and their connections are in the schema served by the Data Gateway . domain: entities: - name: Categories - name: Customers - name: Products - name: Orders - name: Orders.details infrastructure: paths: src: src domain: northwind/domain Query: In this case we will use the Node client ( @lambdaorm/client ), which connects to a Data Gateway to execute the query. And in this case we will write the query in string format. import { orm } from '@lambdaorm/client' import fs from 'fs' import path from'path' ( async () => { try { await orm.init('http://localhost:8080', { headers: { 'X-Api-Key': process.env.BACKEND_KEY } }) // test connection console.log(await orm.general.ping()) // Gets the content of the data.json file to insert the data const content = fs.readFileSync(path.join(__dirname,'../data.json'), 'utf-8') const data = JSON.parse(content) // Import data await orm.stage.import('default',data) // query as string const query = `Orders.filter(p =>p.customerId==customerId) .include(p=>[p.customer.map(p=>p.name),p.details .include(p=>p.product .include(p=>p.category.map(p=>p.name)) .map(p=>p.name)) .map(p=>[p.quantity,p.unitPrice])])` // get plan const plan = await orm.plan(query, { stage: 'default'}) console.log(JSON.stringify(plan,null,2)) // execute query const result = await orm.execute(query, {customerId: 'CENTC' },{ stage: 'default'}) console.log(JSON.stringify(result,null,2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error) } finally { await orm.end() } })() Considerations Keep in mind that whether we use the @lambdaorm/lib or the @lambdaorm/client library we can write the queries in lambda or string format. We could start a development by proposing a simple infrastructure and then make modifications to it and this would not affect our code, since the queries are written based on the domain model and are independent of the infrastructure. You could also have development, test and production environments with different infrastructure configurations without having to alter the code. In addition to the examples presented previously, there are many other use cases that can be solved with λORM by configuring the schema and queries language. Therefore, we invite you to explore the different laboratories and read the documentation .

docs.text: Schema: In the following schema we define 4 entities in the domain: Categories, Customers, Products and Orders, with Orders being an entity composed of Orders and Order Details. In infrastructure we define a single scenario that is associated with a single data source called Ordering, which is a MySQL database, which uses the default mapping. domain: entities: - name: Categories - name: Customers - name: Products - name: Orders - name: Orders.details infrastructure: mappings: - name: default sources: - name: Ordering mapping: default dialect: MySQL connection: ${CNN_MYSQL} stages: - name: default sources: - name: Ordering Query: We will write the query to obtain an Order with its details belonging to a client. We will write the query using lambda expression. import { orm } from 'lambdaorm' import { Orders } from './northwind/domain/model' ( async () => { try { // Initialize the ORM by passing the schema file await orm.init('./lambdaORM.yaml') // Query const query = (customerId:string)=> Orders.filter(p =>p.customerId==customerId) .include(p=>[p.customer.map(p=>p.name),p.details .include(p=>p.product .include(p=>p.category.map(p=>p.name)) .map(p=>p.name)) .map(p=>[p.quantity,p.unitPrice])]) .page(1,1) // Execute the query const result = await orm.execute(query, {customerId: 'CENTC' }) // Print the result console.log(JSON.stringify(result,null,2)) } catch (error: any) { console.error(error) } })() Result: [ { "id": 12, "customerId": "CENTC", "orderDate": "1996-07-18T00:00:00.000Z", "customer": { "name": "Centro comercial Moctezuma" }, "details": [ { "quantity": 10, "unitPrice": 8, "product": { "name": "Sir Rodney's Scones", "category": { "name": "Confections" } } }, { "quantity": 1, "unitPrice": 20.8, "product": { "name": "Gravad lax", "category": { "name": "Seafood" } } } ] } ]

docs.text: Schema: In this case we will define a scenario where the domain entities are persisted in different data sources: The Categories, Products entities are persisted in the source Catalog, which is a MySQL database that uses the default mapping. The Customers entity is persisted in the Crm source, which is a PostgreSQL database that uses the default mapping. The Orders entity is persisted in the Ordering source, which is a MongoDB database that uses the mongoDb mapping. domain: entities: - name: Categories - name: Customers - name: Products - name: Orders - name: Orders.details infrastructure: mappings: - name: default - name: mongoDb extends: default sources: - name: Catalog dialect: MySQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_MYSQL} - name: Crm dialect: PostgreSQL mapping: default connection: ${CNN_POSTGRES} - name: Ordering dialect: MongoDB mapping: mongoDb connection: ${CNN_MONGODB} stages: - name: default sources: - name: Catalog condition: entity.in(["Categories","Products"]) - name: Crm condition: entity.in(["Address","Customers"]) - name: Ordering condition: entity.in(["Orders","Orders.details"]) Query: This time we will execute the query from the command line interface (CLI) and we will obtain the same result as in the previous case. lambdaorm execute -e ".env" -q "Orders.filter(p => p.customerId == customerId).include(p => [p.customer.map(p => p.name), p.details.include(p => p.product.include(p => p.category.map(p => p.name)).map(p => p.name)).map(p => [p.quantity, p.unitPrice])]).page(1,1)" -d "{\"customerId\": \"HANAR\"}" Result: [ { "id": 12, "customerId": "CENTC", "orderDate": "1996-07-18T00:00:00.000Z", "customer": { "name": "Centro comercial Moctezuma" }, "details": [ { "quantity": 10, "unitPrice": 8, "product": { "name": "Sir Rodney's Scones", "category": { "name": "Confections" } } }, { "quantity": 1, "unitPrice": 20.8, "product": { "name": "Gravad lax", "category": { "name": "Seafood" } } } ] } ] view complete laboratory
